richard-francis-burton.name: Richard Francis Burton
richard-francis-burton.summary: British explorer, scholar and army officer (1821–1890) who spoke up to 29 languages, searched for the source of the Nile, made a disguised pilgrimage to Mecca, translated One Thousand and One Nights, and published the Kama Sutra in English.

neo-mamluk-architecture.name: Neo-Mamluk architecture
neo-mamluk-architecture.summary: An architectural style popular in Egypt from the late 19th to early 20th century, blending modern European design with historic Mamluk elements in government buildings, mosques and homes.

luxor-temple.name: Luxor Temple
luxor-temple.summary: A large Ancient Egyptian temple on the Nile at Luxor, built around 1400 BCE and dedicated to the renewal of kingship rather than to a god.

place-de-la-concorde.name: Place de la Concorde
place-de-la-concorde.summary: The largest public square in Paris, at the eastern end of the Champs-Élysées, site of the executions of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette during the French Revolution.

muhammad-ali-of-egypt.name: Muhammad Ali of Egypt
muhammad-ali-of-egypt.summary: An Ottoman governor of Albanian origin who became de facto ruler of Egypt from 1805 to 1848, widely considered the founder of modern Egypt.

pascal-coste.name: Pascal Coste
pascal-coste.summary: A French architect who worked as personal architect to Muhammad Ali Pasha, later becoming chief architect of Marseille in 1844.

cairo-citadel.name: Cairo Citadel
cairo-citadel.summary: A medieval fortress begun by Saladin in 1176, serving as the seat of Egypt's rulers for nearly 700 years until the 19th century.

al-rifa-i-mosque.name: Al-Rifa'i Mosque
al-rifa-i-mosque.summary: A mosque in Cairo near the Citadel, named after a sheikh buried there and serving as the royal mausoleum of Muhammad Ali's family.

max-herz.name: Max Herz
max-herz.summary: Hungarian-born architect, conservator, museum director and architectural historian (1856–1919) who was active in Egypt.

azbakeya.name: Azbakeya
azbakeya.summary: A district formed by Cairo's 19th-century expansion beyond its medieval walls, home to the historic Saint Mark's Coptic Orthodox Cathedral.

pope-of-the-coptic-orthodox-church.name: Pope of Alexandria (Coptic Pope)
pope-of-the-coptic-orthodox-church.summary: Leader of the Coptic Orthodox Church, traditionally the successor to Saint Mark as bishop of Alexandria; the seat has been based in Cairo since 1047.
pope-of-the-coptic-orthodox-church.source_title: Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

giuseppe-verdi.name: Giuseppe Verdi
giuseppe-verdi.summary: An Italian composer (1813–1901) who dominated 19th-century opera, becoming a symbol of Italy's unification movement through works such as Nabucco.

aida.name: Aida
aida.summary: An 1871 opera by Giuseppe Verdi set in ancient Egypt, composed for the opening of Cairo's Khedivial Opera House.

khedive.name: Khedive
khedive.summary: A Persian-origin honorific title used by Ottoman sultans and viziers, and most famously by Egypt's viceroys from 1805 to 1914, first claimed by Muhammad Ali Pasha and officially recognized by the Ottomans in 1867.

ministry-of-endowments-egypt.name: Ministry of Endowments (Egypt)
ministry-of-endowments-egypt.summary: The Egyptian government ministry overseeing religious endowments (awqaf), trust-like arrangements in which a mosque or individual manages property for the community's benefit.

ramses-station.name: Ramses Station
ramses-station.summary: The main railway station of Cairo, Egypt, named for a statue of the pharaoh Ramesses II erected in its square in 1955.

david-roberts-painter.name: David Roberts
david-roberts-painter.summary: Scottish painter (1796–1864) famous for detailed lithographs of Egypt and the Near East made from sketches on his 1838–1840 tours; elected Royal Academician in 1841.

francis-moon.name: F. G. Moon
francis-moon.summary: English printseller and publisher (1796–1871) who also served as Lord Mayor of London.

egyptian-national-library-and-archives.name: Egyptian National Library
egyptian-national-library-and-archives.summary: The largest library in Egypt, holding several million volumes and some of the world's oldest Arabic and Eastern manuscripts, located in Cairo.

museum-of-islamic-art-cairo.name: Museum of Islamic Art, Cairo
museum-of-islamic-art-cairo.summary: Museum in Cairo holding more than 100,000 Islamic artefacts, including rare woodwork, metalwork, ceramics and Qur'an manuscripts, with about 4,500 on display.

ahmed-urabi.name: Ahmed Urabi
ahmed-urabi.summary: Egyptian military officer (1841 to 1911) who rose from the peasantry to lead the 'Urabi revolt against Khedive Tewfik, resulting in British invasion, his capture, and exile to Ceylon.

tewfik-pasha.name: Tewfik Pasha
tewfik-pasha.summary: Khedive of Egypt and Sudan from 1879 to 1892, whose reign saw the anti-foreign Urabi revolt amid financial mismanagement and growing Anglo-French control.

battle-of-gundet.name: Battle of Gundet
battle-of-gundet.summary: A battle fought 14-16 November 1875 in which Ethiopian warriors ambushed and nearly annihilated an Egyptian army in a mountain pass, the first major clash of the Ethiopian-Egyptian War.

battle-of-navarino.name: Battle of Navarino
battle-of-navarino.summary: A naval battle on 20 October 1827 in Navarino Bay, Greece, where British, French and Russian forces destroyed an Ottoman-Egyptian fleet, making Greek independence more likely; the last major sea battle fought entirely by sailing ships.

ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.name: Ibrahim Pasha
ibrahim-pasha-of-egypt.summary: An Egyptian general and the eldest son of Muhammad Ali, who commanded Egyptian and Ottoman armies and briefly ruled Egypt and Sudan as regent before dying only four months later, in 1848.

egyptian-ottoman-war-1831-1833.name: First Turko-Egyptian War
egyptian-ottoman-war-1831-1833.summary: An 1831–1833 war in which Egyptian forces under Muhammad Ali Pasha seized Syria from the Ottoman Empire, a reward he had demanded for earlier military help.

battle-of-nezib.name: Battle of Nezib
battle-of-nezib.summary: An 1839 battle near present-day Nizip, Turkey, in which Egyptian forces led by Ibrahim Pasha defeated the Ottoman army, whose artillery was advised by Prussian officer Helmuth von Moltke the Elder.

battle-of-abukir-1801.name: Battle of Abukir (1801)
battle-of-abukir-1801.summary: An 1801 battle near Egypt's Mediterranean coast in which a British force under Sir Ralph Abercromby landed to fight the French troops remaining after Napoleon's invasion of Egypt.

battle-of-mandora.name: Battle of Mandora
battle-of-mandora.summary: 1801 battle in which French forces failed to stop a British advance toward the French-held port of Alexandria during the campaign to expel France from Egypt.

jacques-fran-ois-menou.name: Menou
jacques-fran-ois-menou.summary: French Army officer and politician (1750–1810) who took part in the French invasion of Egypt and Syria, where he converted to Islam and was renamed Abdallah de Menou.

herbert-kitchener-1st-earl-kitchener.name: Herbert Kitchener
herbert-kitchener-1st-earl-kitchener.summary: British field marshal (1850–1916) who won the Battle of Omdurman in Sudan in 1898, led forces in the Boer War, and organized Britain's volunteer army in the First World War.

mahdist-state.name: Mahdist State
mahdist-state.summary: A Sudanese state formed after Muhammad Ahmad's 1881 uprising against Egyptian rule, which captured Khartoum in 1885 and governed Sudan from Omdurman until defeated by Anglo-Egyptian forces in 1898.

battle-of-omdurman.name: Battle of Omdurman
battle-of-omdurman.summary: A 2 September 1898 battle near Omdurman, Sudan, in which a British-Egyptian force under Herbert Kitchener defeated the Mahdist army of Abdallahi ibn Muhammad, demonstrating modern weapons' superiority; Winston Churchill took part.

thaddeus-p-mott.name: Thaddeus P. Mott
thaddeus-p-mott.summary: American soldier of fortune and former Union Army officer who fought in several countries' wars and recruited American veterans to modernize the Egyptian army in the 1870s.

henry-hopkins-sibley.name: Henry Hopkins Sibley
henry-hopkins-sibley.summary: US Army officer (1816 to 1886) who later commanded a Confederate cavalry brigade in the Civil War, notably in a failed 1862 New Mexico campaign.

william-wing-loring.name: William Wing Loring
william-wing-loring.summary: An American soldier, politician, and lawyer who served in the U.S., Confederate, and Egyptian armies; a Mexican-American War veteran and one of the Army's youngest colonels, he was later made a Fereek Pasha in Egypt (1818–1886).

diriyah.name: Diriyah
diriyah.summary: Town near Riyadh that was the original home of the House of Saud and capital of the first Saudi state from 1727 to 1818; its old district is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abdullah-bin-saud-al-saud.name: Abdullah bin Saud Al Saud
abdullah-bin-saud-al-saud.summary: Last ruler of the First Saudi State, reigning 1814–1818, executed in Istanbul by the Ottomans after their conquest ended his rule.

charles-napier-royal-navy-officer.name: Charles Napier
charles-napier-royal-navy-officer.summary: British admiral and politician (1786–1860) who served sixty years in the Royal Navy, briefly commanded the Portuguese Navy, and was among the naval officers most widely known to the public in the early Victorian era.

jounieh.name: Jounieh
jounieh.summary: Coastal city in Lebanon north of Beirut, known for its seaside resorts, old stone souk and a gondola lift up to the Our Lady of Lebanon shrine.

funj-sultanate.name: Funj Sultanate
funj-sultanate.summary: An Islamic kingdom in what is now Sudan, founded in 1504 by Sultan Amara Dunqas at its capital Sennar, reaching its peak in the late 17th century before an 1821 Turco-Egyptian conquest ended it.

sennar.name: Sennar
sennar.summary: A city on the Blue Nile in Sudan that served for centuries as capital of the Funj Kingdom of Sennar and later of Sennar State.

badi-vii.name: Badi VII
badi-vii.summary: The last ruler of the Funj Sultanate, reigning 1805 to 1821, who surrendered his capital Sennar to invading Egyptian forces under Ismail Pasha without resistance.

battle-of-gura.name: Battle of Gura
battle-of-gura.summary: The decisive second major battle of the Ethiopian-Egyptian War, fought 7-10 March 1876 near Gura in Eritrea, ending in Egyptian defeat.

percy-bysshe-shelley.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
percy-bysshe-shelley.summary: An English Romantic poet (1792–1822), little recognized in his lifetime but hugely influential afterward, known for works such as 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode to the West Wind'.

ozymandias.name: Ozymandias
ozymandias.summary: A sonnet by English Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, first published in 1818, about the ruined legacy of a great Egyptian pharaoh.

mohammed-hussein-heikal.name: Muhammad Husayn Haykal
mohammed-hussein-heikal.summary: Egyptian writer, journalist and politician (1888–1956) who wrote the first Arabic-language novel and held several cabinet posts, including minister of education.

zaynab-novel.name: Zaynab
zaynab-novel.summary: A 1913 novel by Muhammad Husayn Haykal often considered the first Arabic novel, depicting Egyptian countryside life and romantic relationships across social classes.

jean-fran-ois-champollion.name: Jean-François Champollion
jean-fran-ois-champollion.summary: A French philologist (1790–1832) who deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs, becoming a founding figure of Egyptology after studying the trilingual Rosetta Stone.

thomas-young-scientist.name: Thomas Young
thomas-young-scientist.summary: A British polymath (1773–1829) who helped decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs on the Rosetta Stone and established the wave theory of light.

the-holy-land-syria-idumea-arabia-egypt-.name: The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia
the-holy-land-syria-idumea-arabia-egypt-.summary: A travelogue of Palestine and the Middle East with 250 lithographs by Louis Haghe after David Roberts's watercolors, published by subscription from 1842 to 1849.
the-holy-land-syria-idumea-arabia-egypt-.source_title: The Holy Land, Syria, Idumea, Arabia, Egypt, and Nubia

louis-haghe.name: Louis Haghe
louis-haghe.summary: A lithographer and watercolourist (1806–1885), from the Netherlands and later Britain, who pioneered colour lithography and produced 250 images for David Roberts's Holy Land travelogue.

rosetta.name: Rosetta
rosetta.summary: A Nile Delta port city in Egypt, near where the Rosetta Stone was found in 1799; founded around the 9th century, it later became a popular 19th-century British tourist stop.

emmanuel-de-roug.name: Emmanuel de Rougé
emmanuel-de-roug.summary: A French Egyptologist and philologist (1811–1872), member of the House of Rougé.

muhammad-abduh.name: Muhammad Abduh
muhammad-abduh.summary: An Egyptian Islamic scholar and judge who served as Grand Mufti of Egypt and was a central figure of the Islamic modernism and Arab Nahda movements of the late 1800s and early 1900s.

jamal-al-din-al-afghani.name: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani
jamal-al-din-al-afghani.summary: A political activist and Islamic ideologist (1838/39-1897) who was one of the founders of Islamic Modernism and advocated Pan-Islamic unity in India against the British.

al-urwah-al-wuthqa.name: Al-Urwah al-Wuthqa
al-urwah-al-wuthqa.summary: A pan-Islamic revolutionary journal founded in 1884 by Muhammad Abduh and Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, banned by Britain for opposing European colonialism.

nahda.name: Nahda
nahda.summary: A 19th- and early 20th-century cultural 'awakening' that flourished in Arab regions of the Ottoman Empire, especially Egypt, Syria and Lebanon.

almah-dancer.name: Almah
almah-dancer.summary: Class of educated Egyptian women trained to sing and recite classical Arabic poetry, who performed at weddings and festivities without displaying themselves.

edward-william-lane.name: Edward William Lane
edward-william-lane.summary: British orientalist, translator and lexicographer (1801–1876) known for his account of Egyptian customs and his translation of One Thousand and One Nights.

george-croly.name: George Croly
george-croly.summary: Irish poet, novelist, historian and Anglican priest (1780–1860) who served as rector of St Stephen Walbrook in London from 1835 until his death.

annabel-j-wharton.name: Annabel Wharton
annabel-j-wharton.summary: American art historian specializing in Byzantine and Late Ancient art and architecture, currently a professor at Duke University.

institut-d-gypte.name: Institut d'Égypte
institut-d-gypte.summary: A scientific research institute in Cairo founded in 1798 and specializing in Egyptology, the second-oldest such institute in Egypt after Al-Azhar University.

isma-il-pasha-of-egypt.name: Isma'il Pasha
isma-il-pasha-of-egypt.summary: Khedive of Egypt and ruler of Sudan from 1863 to 1879, known as Ismail the Magnificent, who invested heavily in industry and urbanization but left Egypt deeply in debt, leading to his removal by Britain and France.

anglo-egyptian-war.name: Anglo-Egyptian War
anglo-egyptian-war.summary: The 1882 conflict between Egyptian and Sudanese forces under Ahmed 'Urabi and the United Kingdom, ending in a British takeover and occupation of Egypt.

hejaz.name: Hejaz
hejaz.summary: A historical region of western Arabia, in modern Saudi Arabia, containing the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, the first and second holiest sites in Islam.

sultanate-of-darfur.name: Sultanate of Darfur
sultanate-of-darfur.summary: Pre-colonial state in present-day Sudan lasting from the 16th century to 1874, stretching at its peak from Darfur to the White Nile.

mahdi.name: Mahdi
mahdi.summary: An Islamic messianic figure expected to appear before the End Times to restore justice alongside Jesus; central to Shia theology, where he is identified with the twelfth Imam, born in 869 CE and in occultation.

ansar-sudan.name: Ansar
ansar-sudan.summary: Sufi religious movement in Sudan whose followers are disciples of Muhammad Ahmad, who proclaimed himself Mahdi in 1881. His followers captured Khartoum in 1885, and his descendants have led the movement since.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

urabi-revolt.name: Urabi revolution
urabi-revolt.summary: A nationalist uprising in Egypt from 1879 to 1882 led by Colonel Ahmed Urabi against the khedive and British and French influence, ended when Britain invaded.

sublime-porte.name: Sublime Porte
sublime-porte.summary: A term for the central government of the Ottoman Empire in Istanbul, referring to the building that housed the Grand Vizier's office and other key ministries.

abbas-ii-of-egypt.name: Abbas II of Egypt
abbas-ii-of-egypt.summary: The last Khedive of Egypt and Sudan, ruling from 1892 to 1914, deposed by the British as a nationalist in favor of his more pro-British uncle after the Ottoman Empire joined World War I against Britain.

hussein-kamel-of-egypt.name: Hussein Kamel
hussein-kamel-of-egypt.summary: Sultan of Egypt from 1914 to 1917 during the British protectorate, the first to hold that title since 1517.

rifa-a-at-tahtawi.name: Rifa'a at-Tahtawi
rifa-a-at-tahtawi.summary: Egyptian writer, teacher, translator and intellectual (1801–1873) of the Arab renaissance. He published an account of his five years in France in 1834 and founded a School of Languages in Cairo in 1835.

tienne-bonnot-de-condillac.name: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac
tienne-bonnot-de-condillac.summary: French philosopher and Catholic priest (1714 to 1780) who focused on psychology and the philosophy of the mind.

voltaire.name: Voltaire
voltaire.summary: Pen name of French Enlightenment writer and philosopher François-Marie Arouet (1694-1778), a prolific author known for criticizing the Church and advocating freedom of speech and religion.

jean-jacques-rousseau.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
jean-jacques-rousseau.summary: A Genevan philosopher and writer (1712–1778) whose political ideas, including in The Social Contract, shaped the Enlightenment and the French Revolution.

montesquieu.name: Montesquieu
montesquieu.summary: French political philosopher (1689 to 1755) known for developing the theory of separation of powers and for his 1748 book The Spirit of Law, which influenced the US Constitution.

al-azhar-university.name: Al-Azhar University
al-azhar-university.summary: Founded in Cairo in 970 by the Fatimid Caliphate, it is Egypt's oldest university and one of the most prestigious centers of Islamic learning in the world.

islamic-modernism.name: Islamic modernism
islamic-modernism.summary: Movement that emerged in the mid-19th century in reaction to Western dominance and colonialism. It re-reads the Qur'an and Sunna in their historical context and embraces modern European institutions, unlike Salafism or Islamism.

qasim-amin.name: Qasim Amin
qasim-amin.summary: Egyptian jurist and Islamic modernist (1863–1908), a founder of the Egyptian national movement and co-founder of Cairo University. His call for women's rights sparked debate across the Arab world.

napoleon.name: Napoleon
napoleon.summary: French emperor from 1804 to 1814, and briefly in 1815, who rose to power as a general during the French Revolution and led sweeping military campaigns across Europe and the Middle East.

hasan-al-attar.name: Hasan al-Attar
hasan-al-attar.summary: Scholar (1766–1835) who was Grand Imam of al-Azhar from 1830 to 1835. He wrote on grammar, science, medicine and history, and was an early reformist cleric in Ottoman Egypt.

charles-darwin.name: Charles Darwin
charles-darwin.summary: English naturalist and biologist (1809-1882) known for his theory of evolution by natural selection, described as one of history's most influential figures.

herbert-spencer.name: Herbert Spencer
herbert-spencer.summary: English polymath (1820–1903) who coined the phrase "survival of the fittest" and applied evolution to sociology and ethics. He was hugely famous in the late 19th century, but his influence faded after 1900.

john-stuart-mill.name: John Stuart Mill
john-stuart-mill.summary: English philosopher and politician (1806–1873), a leading liberal thinker who championed individual liberty, women's rights and utilitarianism, author of On Liberty.

temple-of-dendur.name: Temple of Dendur
temple-of-dendur.summary: A Roman-era Egyptian temple built around 23 BCE for the goddess Isis, rescued from Nile flooding in the 1960s and given to New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art.

armar-lowry-corry.name: Armar Lowry Corry
armar-lowry-corry.summary: British naval officer (1793–1855) who rose to the rank of rear-admiral.

girolamo-segato.name: Girolamo Segato
girolamo-segato.summary: An Italian naturalist, cartographer and Egyptologist (1792–1836) best known for a technique that 'petrified' human cadavers, preserving their color and texture.

peteese-and-pihor.name: Pihor
peteese-and-pihor.summary: One of two Nubian brothers believed to have drowned in the Nile and become minor gods in Egypt's 26th dynasty; a temple to him, his brother and Isis was built at Dendur.

war-of-the-second-coalition.name: War of the Second Coalition
war-of-the-second-coalition.summary: An 1798–1802 war pitting revolutionary France against a coalition led by Britain, Austria and Russia, ending with French territorial gains confirmed and Austria compensated with Venetia.

anglo-egyptian-conquest-of-sudan.name: Anglo-Egyptian conquest of Sudan
anglo-egyptian-conquest-of-sudan.summary: The 1896-1899 British-Egyptian military campaign that defeated the Mahdist State and restored Anglo-Egyptian rule over Sudan, lasting until Sudan's independence in 1956.

abdul-hamid-ii.name: Abdul Hamid II
abdul-hamid-ii.summary: 34th sultan of the Ottoman Empire (1876–1909), the last to hold effective control over the fracturing state, who suspended the constitution in 1878 and ruled with absolute power.

greco-turkish-war-1897.name: Greco-Turkish War of 1897
greco-turkish-war-1897.summary: A brief 1897 war between Greece and the Ottoman Empire over the status of Crete; despite Ottoman victory on the battlefield, Crete gained autonomy the following year.

cretan-muslims.name: Cretan Muslims
cretan-muslims.summary: Greek Muslim inhabitants of Crete descended from Orthodox Greeks who converted to Islam after the Ottoman conquest of the island; many later resettled in Turkey, the Levant, and North Africa.
